questions.q: What does an SCD Type 1 change do?
options: Overwrites the existing dimension row's value in place, keeping no history of the old value
Inserts a brand-new row with a new surrogate key, preserving the old row unchanged
Adds a new column to store the previous value alongside the current one
Deletes the dimension member entirely
questions.explain: Type 1 is the overwrite pattern: the existing row is updated directly, the surrogate key stays the same, and the old value leaves no trace.

questions.q: In the real Microsoft diagram used in this lesson, what change is made to salesperson Rachel Valdez's row (surrogate key 295)?
options: Her phone number is updated from 555-1234 to 555-6789, in the same row
A new row with surrogate key 369 is inserted for her
Her SalesRegion_FK is duplicated into a PreviousSalesRegion_FK column
Her record is flagged with IsCurrent = FALSE
questions.explain: The diagram shows a straightforward overwrite: same surrogate key 295, phone number changed in place from 555-1234 to 555-6789 — no new row, no history columns involved.

questions.q: According to Microsoft's own guidance, when should SCD Type 1 be used?
options: For most changing attributes, especially corrections like a misspelled name or a typo'd phone number
Only for attributes that must legally retain full historical records
Never — Type 1 should always be replaced with Type 2
Only for the surrogate key column itself
questions.explain: Microsoft's guidance describes Type 1 as the right choice for most changing attributes and for correcting errors, reserving Type 2 for attributes that specifically need historical perspective preserved.

questions.q: What real consequence does a Type 1 overwrite have on historical reporting?
options: Historical facts joined to that dimension row now report using the new value, as if it had always been true
Historical facts become permanently unqueryable
The fact table's grain automatically changes to match the new attribute value
There is no consequence — Type 1 changes never affect any reports
questions.explain: Because the old value is gone and the surrogate key is unchanged, every fact that joins to that row — past and future — now reflects the new value, retroactively rewriting historical rollups.

questions.q: How many SQL statements does a basic Type 1 update require?
options: One UPDATE statement targeting the existing surrogate key
Two statements: an UPDATE followed by an INSERT
Three statements: a DELETE, an INSERT, and an UPDATE
Zero — Type 1 changes require no SQL at all
questions.explain: Type 1 is a single UPDATE against the existing row — its simplicity, compared to Type 2's UPDATE-plus-INSERT pattern, is exactly why it's the lower-effort default.
